source: Roberts, Teoh, Hutcherson (2022) Time to Pay Attention? Information Search Explains Amplified Framing Effects Under Time Pressure
finding: Preregistered direct replication of Guo et al. (2017): a 1-second limit made the gain/loss framing gap larger. The rise came only from gain-framed trials, where people took the sure option more. Loss-framed choices did not change with time.
numbers: 2x2 within-subject (frame x 1 s limit vs none). Behaviour N=45 (df 44), eye-tracking N=40. Gamble choice, limited time: gain .34, loss .64, d=1.52. Unlimited time: gain .52, loss .64, d=0.75. Frame x time F(1,44)=57.06, etaG2=.06. Time effect in gain frame d=1.32; in loss frame d=0.003 (p=.98).
quote: the framing effect was larger when participants had limited time
limits: Small student sample; one task (pie-chart gambles). Reanalysis of Diederich 2020 and Guo 2017 also showed a weaker time effect in loss frames.
agent_relevance: Time pressure is not a simple 'more bias' dial. The effect is asymmetric by frame, so a cleaned prompt matters most when the agent must answer fast.

source: Roberts et al. (2022): attention account of the time-pressure effect (same paper, mechanism)
finding: Rival to the dual-system reading. Under time pressure the first fixation went to the reward-colored option, and search was cut short. That alone can produce a larger framing effect without a 'fast System 1' override.
numbers: First fixation on gamble: gain frame .42 (unlimited) vs .32 (limited); loss frame .58 vs .60. Frame x time on first fixation F(1,39)=20.63. Probability x time interaction on first look b=0.72, p=.003.
limits: Eye tracking shows the account is sufficient, not that dual systems are wrong. N=40.
agent_relevance: Truncated information search, not lost reasoning, may drive time-pressure bias. An agent that must act on little context should have its frame fixed in what it is shown first.

source: Gong, Wang, Ma, Lv (2026) How Time Pressure Amplifies Framing Effects in Risky Decision-Making
finding: Two eye-tracking experiments with a 1 s limit. Time pressure cut fixation counts and durations, and pushed choices toward the frame-consistent option, even flipping risk preference by frame. Spatial position of the sure option did not moderate the time effect; presentation order did in loss frames.
numbers: Exp 1: 30 recruited, df 25 so about 26 analysed. Risky choice, gain frame: .11 under pressure vs .36 without. Loss frame: .85 vs .49. Time x frame F(1,25)=309.50, etap2=.93. Frame main effect F(1,25)=282.58, etap2=.92. Under pressure plus loss frame, more risk seeking when the sure option came second.
limits: Very large effect sizes in a tiny sample, so possibly easy task. Loss-frame change differs from Roberts 2022, where loss choices did not move.
agent_relevance: Order of options in a prompt is itself a moderator under compressed budgets. Randomise or code-check option order.

source: Bialek (2023) Why Should We Study the Foreign Language Effect: Debiasing through Affecting Metacognition?
finding: Review of the foreign-language effect (FLE). Early work found less framing and more risk-taking in a foreign language (Keysar 2012; Costa 2014). Later work is mixed: several labs found no FLE on risky choice or on heuristics-and-biases tasks. Proposed mechanisms (less emotion, more reflection, abstract construal) are not consistently confirmed.
numbers: No new N. Cites: no FLE on risky choice (Borkowska 2023; Muda 2020); no effect on heuristics tasks (Maekelae and Pfuhl 2019; Vives 2018); CRT equal in native and foreign language (Costa 2014; Milczarski 2022; Vega-Mendoza 2021). Arousal did not predict the decision change (Geipel 2015; Hadjichristidis 2015; Muda 2023).
quote: the effect appears more complex and malleable than initially hoped
limits: Author is a co-author of some null results. Narrative review, not a meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Do not count on 'prompt in another language' as a debiaser. Evidence is weak and mixed. Test it on our own tasks before using it.

source: Keysar, Hayakawa, An (2012) The foreign-language effect: thinking in a foreign tongue reduces decision biases
finding: Four experiments: the Asian-disease framing effect disappeared when choices were given in a foreign tongue. Two more showed less loss aversion (more acceptance of positive-expected-value bets).
numbers: Abstract only read (via Europe PMC). Exact cell sizes and percentages not read.
limits: Abstract level only. Later replications are mixed (see b04, b06, b07).
agent_relevance: The founding claim for 'second language weakens framing'. Treat as a hypothesis, not a reliable lever.

source: Hayakawa, Lau, Holtzmann, Costa, Keysar (2019) On the reliability of the foreign language effect on risk-taking
finding: Four experiments, mixed results. Exp 1: foreign language increased strategic risk-taking. Exp 2 and 3: no effect of language nativeness on risk-taking. Exp 4: foreign language raised risk-taking in general.
numbers: Abstract only read. Per-experiment N not read.
limits: Abstract level only. A partial replication from the original lab.
agent_relevance: Even the original lab could not reproduce a stable direction. Low trust in language switching as a control.

source: Stibbard-Hawkes et al. (2024) Foreign-language effects in cross-cultural behavioral research: Evidence from the Tanzanian Hadza
finding: Hadza adults were randomly given tasks in their first language (Hadzane) or Kiswahili. Non-native language made people more utilitarian in sacrificial dilemmas, but it decreased risk preference in wager and Likert tasks, the opposite of the classic FLE direction.
numbers: N=129. Tasks: dictator game, two sacrificial dilemmas, wager task, five Likert risk measures. Authors call the wager effect moderate and the dilemma and Likert effects substantial (exact estimates not extracted).
limits: No framing task. Culture, linguistic relativity and language context may explain the reversal. Fluency had only a minor effect.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the FLE sign is not universal. A language trick may help or hurt depending on population.

source: Zhen and Yu (2016) All framing effects are not created equal: Low convergent validity between two classic measurements of framing
finding: Two classic framing tasks (vignette, Asian-disease type, and reward-based gambling) barely correlate within the same person. The framing effect is shaped by task domain (gain vs loss) and context, so it is not one stable trait.
numbers: N=159 young adults (151 in correlations). Vignette loss domain vs gambling gain domain: rs=0.056, p=.498. Gambling vs vignette, pooled domains: rs=0.167, p=.040. Gain vs loss domain in gambling r=0.164; in vignette rs=0.178. Gambling vs vignette loss domain rs=0.144, p=.078; gain domain rs=0.027.
limits: Young adult sample, one lab. Shows poor convergent validity, not zero effect.
agent_relevance: Individual-difference moderators of framing are hard to pin down because 'framing susceptibility' is task-specific. Expect the same for an LLM: measure per task.

source: Individual differences moderate effects in an Unusual Disease paradigm: A psychophysical data collection approach (2023)
finding: Risk style moderated the gain/loss framing effect in both studies. Cognitive style (intuitive vs deliberate) moderated it only in the larger online study. Number of frame-inconsistent choices was unrelated to either style.
numbers: Study 1: N=43, 480 trials each. Study 2: N=262, 80 trials each. Also varied number affected, probabilities, disease type and response deadlines.
limits: Two scales of cognitive style gave different answers; Study 1 and 2 effects differ. Not a CRT study.
agent_relevance: Thinking-style traits are an unreliable predictor of who is framed. Do not assume a 'more deliberate' mode removes framing.

source: Robinson, Rosenzweig, Moss, Litman (2019) Tapped out or barely tapped? Harnessing the unused potential of the Mechanical Turk participant pool
finding: Asian-disease framing effect was about the same size in experienced and inexperienced MTurk workers. Participant naivete did not weaken it.
numbers: Condition effect (% choosing program A, positive minus negative frame): standard sample 32.3 points, inexperienced 36.4 points. Group x condition not significant (logistic OR=-1.14, p=.80).
limits: Online sample; the paper is about sampling, framing is a side check.
agent_relevance: Familiarity with the problem does not remove framing. A model that has seen the Asian-disease text may still be framed, so test with novel scenarios.

source: Cheung, Maier, Lieder (2025) Large language models show amplified cognitive biases in moral decision-making (PNAS)
finding: LLMs endorsed inaction more than people (omission bias) and were pushed by wording: flipping the yes/no polarity of a question flipped their answer. Fine-tuning for chat appears to cause it.
numbers: Study 1: N=285 humans, 22 dilemmas. Study 2: N=474 (prereg). Study 3: N=491 (prereg, Reddit-style dilemmas). Omission bias vs people: GPT-4-turbo F(1,963)=28.47, etap2=.03; Llama 3.1-Instruct F=33.23, etap2=.03; Claude 3.5 F=60.48, etap2=.06; GPT-4o not different (F=1.39, p=.239) but at ceiling in 5 of 6 vignettes. Pretrained Llama 3.1 and Centaur did not show the yes-no bias.
quote: LLMs tend to answer "no," thus flipping their decision/advice depending on how the question is worded.
limits: Moral dilemmas, not gain-loss framing. 2024-era models. GPT-4o ceiling limits the comparison.
agent_relevance: Question polarity and action-vs-omission wording move LLM answers more than human answers. Code should restate the question in both polarities and compare.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 showed the gain/loss framing effect (plus certainty effect and overweighting), but not the reflection, isolation or magnitude-perception effects. Tested with the original Kahneman and Tversky problem pairs.
numbers: Choice probabilities (temperature 1) turned into log-odds ratios between paired problems; option order counterbalanced. GPT-3 showed 3 of 6 tested biases. Exact log-odds values not extracted.
limits: GPT-3 (davinci-era), not current models; classic vignettes are likely in training data.
agent_relevance: Older LLMs are framed by classic tasks, so framing is a live risk for any prompt we pass in.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The emergence of economic rationality of GPT (PNAS)
finding: GPT was highly rational on budget choices across risk, time, social and food tasks, but rationality fell sharply when prices were reframed ('Y points = 1 unit' instead of '1 point = X units'). Humans also dropped, less than GPT.
numbers: 10,000 GPT tasks (100 repeats per environment) vs N=347 humans. Price-framing CCEI: risk 0.901 (34% below 0.9), time 0.884 (48%), social 0.698 (88%), food 0.894 (49%). Baseline CCEI significantly higher in each domain (p<.01). Demand-slope correlations under reframing: -0.053, -0.116, 0.267, -0.499. Drop larger for GPT than humans (OLS).
limits: Budget-allocation framing, not gain-loss. Single model family. Temperature 0 baseline.
agent_relevance: Equivalent re-descriptions of the same numbers can cut an LLM's consistency; a cleaned canonical form of inputs is worth the cost.

source: Germani, Spitale et al. (2025) Source framing triggers systematic bias in large language models (Science Advances)
finding: Four LLMs agree highly with each other when judging statements blind. Agreement breaks when the author is named. Attributing to a Chinese person lowers agreement across models, most for DeepSeek Reasoner.
numbers: 4,800 statements, 24 topics, 192,000 assessments. Blind: DeepSeek Reasoner on Grok 2 text 56.3% agreement vs 91.7% with itself. Anti-Chinese bias vs blind: Grok 2 -14.22% (p<.001), Mistral -4.51% (ns), o3-mini -2.64% (p<.001). Same Taiwan statement scored 50% blind but 0% when misattributed to DeepSeek. LLM-attributed text scored slightly lower (Mistral -0.85%, DeepSeek -0.53%, Grok 2 -0.34%).
limits: Source attribution is a credibility cue, not a gain-loss frame. Direction varies by topic (Gaza reversed).
agent_relevance: Source labels act as a framing moderator on LLM judges. Strip authorship before judging, as guardrail G5 already says.

source: Susceptibility of Large Language Models to User-Driven Factors in Medical Queries (2026)
finding: Misinformation framing, authority of its source and assertive tone lowered diagnostic accuracy. Proprietary models fell more under strong or authoritative misinformation. Dropping exam and lab findings caused the largest accuracy loss.
numbers: MedQA test split 1,273 questions plus Medbullets 308. Perturbation test (persona, source authority, tone) and ablation of key clinical data. Per-model accuracy numbers not extracted (in figures).
limits: Misinformation, not equivalent re-description. Numbers only in figures.
agent_relevance: Credible-sounding wrong framing hurts LLMs. This is the mirror of Druckman's human result, where credible advice helps.

source: Take caution in using LLMs as human surrogates (PNAS, 2025)
finding: Position paper: LLM answers are brittle to small prompt wording changes and option order, so LLM-as-subject results about human biases may not generalise.
numbers: No new experiment read; cites prompt brittleness from spaces, control characters and option order.
limits: Position paper; authors not verified.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording is a nuisance variable we must control.

source: Druckman (2001) Using credible advice to overcome framing effects (J Law Econ Organ 17:62-82)
finding: In two experiments, some well-known framing effects greatly diminish and sometimes disappear when participants get credible advice on how to decide. The claim is that earlier work overstates framing because people chose in isolation.
numbers: Abstract page only (paywall). No N, percentages or conditions read.
quote: some widely known framing effects greatly diminish and sometimes disappear
limits: Paywalled; details not verified. The credibility manipulation is the source of advice, which a prompt can only mimic.
agent_relevance: Core claim for the subfield. Needs a full read before we cite numbers.

source: Wikipedia, Framing effect (psychology): moderators section (secondary summary)
finding: Lists moderators and citations: Druckman 2001b (credible information reduces or removes framing); Roberts 2022 (time pressure); Keysar 2012 (foreign language); Bizer 2013 (depth of processing); Thomas and Millar 2011 (analytic processing); age effects (Xu 2024).
numbers: Hershfield, Shu, Benartzi 2020 field test: about 30% enrolled under '$5 a day' vs about 7% under '$150 a month'. Krishnamurthy and Hu 2026: N=907 vaccine-hesitant adults; 'protect others' frame raised acceptance at all hesitancy levels.
limits: Secondary source; numbers as stated there, not re-checked.
agent_relevance: A citation map to chase. Real-world frame choice can move behaviour about 4x.

source: Strough, Karns, Schlosnagle (2011) Decision-making heuristics and biases across the life span
finding: Review of the sunk-cost fallacy and the framing effect across ages. Framing appears relatively stable across the life span; sunk-cost falls with age.
numbers: Abstract only read. No numbers.
limits: Conflicts with newer work reporting more framing in older adults (Xu 2024, via Wikipedia). Not resolved here.
agent_relevance: Age moderation is unsettled; no direct agent use.

source: Peters et al. (2009) How numeracy influences risk comprehension and medical decision making
finding: Low numeracy raises susceptibility to framing, ratio bias, mood and format effects.
numbers: Abstract only read.
limits: Abstract level; effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Skill with numbers is a moderator: when numbers are explicit and computed, framing should fall. Supports code-side arithmetic.

source: Costa et al. (2014) Your Morals Depend on Language (PLoS ONE)
finding: Foreign language made footbridge-dilemma answers more utilitarian. Authors tie it to reduced emotion. Not a framing task, but the same lab line as Keysar 2012.
numbers: Experiment 1 weighted across populations: utilitarian choice 20% native vs 33% foreign, chi2(1,N=317)=6.9, p<.01. Differences ranged 7.5 to 65 points by population. Second sample: native N=158, foreign N=159.
limits: Moral dilemma, not framing. Later FLE-moral studies are mixed (see b04).
agent_relevance: Language changes emotional distance; unclear if an LLM has an analogue.

source: Cross-linguistic patterns of cognitive biases in large language models: English, Hebrew, Russian (Front AI, 2026)
finding: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini beat humans on a rule-based deductive task but showed bias-mimicking errors on heuristic tasks (availability, confirmation). Effects varied by language and model.
numbers: 2,028 observations: 507 human, 1,521 LLM. Three languages, three models. Chi-square, Bonferroni, Firth logistic regression.
limits: Availability and confirmation bias, not framing. Only abstract and intro read in detail.
agent_relevance: Input language changes LLM bias rates unpredictably: do not assume English results transfer.
